title: Κύων καὶ μάγειρος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 183. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κύων εἰσπηδήσας εἰς μαγειρεῖον καί, τοῦ μαγείρου ἀσχολουμένου, καρδίαν ἁρπάσας, ἔφυγεν.
sentences.tr: Kyōn eispēdēsas eis mageireion kai, tou mageirou ascholoumenou, kardian harpasas, ephygen.
sentences.l: A dog, having leapt into a cook-shop and, the cook being occupied, having snatched a heart, fled.
sentences.i: A dog leapt into a cookshop and, while the cook was busy, snatched up a heart and ran.
sentences.n: μαγειρεῖον is the cook's shop, where meat was butchered and dressed for sale. τοῦ μαγείρου ἀσχολουμένου is a genitive absolute giving the moment. καρδία here is the animal's heart as a cut of meat.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ μάγειρος ἐπιστραφείς, ὡς εἶδεν αὐτὸν φεύγοντα, εἶπεν· « Ὦ οὗτος, ἴσθι ὡς, ὅπουπερ ἂν ᾖς, φυλάξομαί σε· οὐ γὰρ ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ καρδίαν εἴληφας, ἀλλ’ ἐμοὶ καρδίαν ἔδωκας. »
sentences.tr: Ho de mageiros epistrapheis, hōs eiden auton pheugonta, eipen· « Ō houtos, isthi hōs, hopouper an ēis, phylaxomai se· ou gar ap’ emou kardian eilēphas, all’ emoi kardian edōkas. »
sentences.l: And the cook, having turned round, when he saw him fleeing, said: « You there, know that, wherever you may be, I shall guard myself against you; for you have not taken a heart from me, but you have given me a heart. »
sentences.i: The cook turned round, and when he saw him making off he said: « You there — be sure that wherever you are, I shall be on my guard against you; you have not taken a heart from me, you have given me one. »
sentences.n: The close turns on one word doing two jobs: καρδία is the meat that was stolen and the courage the cook is left with. ἴσθι here is the imperative of οἶδα, 'know', not of εἰμί. ὅπουπερ ἄν with the subjunctive is a general 'wherever at all'. φυλάξομαι is the middle of φυλάσσω, 'guard oneself against', taking the accusative of the thing feared.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλάκις τὰ παθήματα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις μαθήματα γίνονται.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti pollakis ta pathēmata tois anthrōpois mathēmata ginontai.
sentences.l: The fable shows that often sufferings become lessons for men.
sentences.n: παθήματα μαθήματα is a proverbial jingle — what is suffered and what is learnt, the two words a single letter apart — and Greek liked it well enough to keep it as a saying on its own. τοῖς ἀνθρώποις is a dative of the person concerned.
